Just now

--

Gary Vaynerchuk’s argument about the return to real life made me look again at the business I have been building.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Technology can help organize and carry the work, but observation, judgment, and human experience are what give it meaning.Gary Vaynerchuk’s July 24 LinkedIn newsletter, titled: The Pendulum Is Swinging Back to Real Life, did not make me want to open a café, start a running club, or bring back the drive-in movie theater.
It made me look more closely at my own business.
His argument was that the rapid growth of artificial intelligence will not make the physical world less important. It may do the opposite. As technology becomes faster, more capable, and more deeply embedded in daily life, people will place greater value on experiences that feel physical, personal, and difficult to reproduce.
He described it as a barbell. Extreme technology sits at one end. Deeply human, real-life experience sits at the other. The comfortable middle, where average digital work and average physical experiences once survived, begins to disappear.
The more I considered that argument, the more I realized that it also describes the future of my work.
Through Whyte-Hall Communications Network, I audit real estate communication and publish what I find. Then clients hire me to write theirs. On the surface, that may sound like a writing business. In reality, the writing is only the visible part of the work.
The real work begins with observation.
Observation came before the business
Long before artificial intelligence entered the conversation, I developed the habit of watching people.
During my years in journalism back in tropical isle of Jamaica, I would sometimes position myself in busy places such as Half Way Tree, Parade, downtown Kingston, or Cross Roads and simply observe.
I watched how people moved, how they spoke, what caught their attention, what they ignored, and how they reacted to one another. I was not always looking for a particular story. Sometimes I was learning how people behaved when nobody was interviewing them.
That habit became part of how I approached journalism. Later, it followed me into public relations, corporate communications, and the work I now do with real estate professionals.
I still watch people, although much of the observation now happens through documents, for example:

• I read listing descriptions and notice where the property disappears beneath familiar phrases.

• I examine agent biographies and find years of experience listed without any explanation of how that experience helps a client.

• I review “Just Sold” posts and see the same celebration repeated so often that the actual work behind the closing is lost.

• I study brokerage websites, press releases, client letters, LinkedIn profiles, market updates, and deal summaries, looking for the place where the reader has to stop and guess.
That is my version of standing in the store.
Gary wrote that the store was always the studio. His early business ideas and content grew out of his time inside his father’s wine shop, where he spent his days speaking with customers and learning what they cared about.
For me, the real estate industry is the studio.
The documents are the raw material. The conversations provide context. The recurring communication failures become subjects for investigation. The findings become articles, newsletter posts, comments, case histories, and services.
The content does not create the work.
The work creates the content.
AI can produce words. It cannot decide what matters.
Artificial intelligence has made writing faster.
It can produce a listing description, an agent profile, a press release, a social media post, or a client email in seconds. It can summarize information, reorganize paragraphs, identify repeated words, and offer several versions of the same message.
I use AI, and I expect its role in my business to continue growing.
But the ability to generate language is not the same as the ability to understand what needs to be said.
Before a useful listing description can be written, someone must determine which property details matter, what information buyers are likely to misunderstand, and what makes the home different from the competing inventory.
Before an agent biography can become credible, someone must ask what the agent actually does, which clients the agent serves best, what experience has shaped the work, and why any of that should matter to a prospective client.
Before a closing can become a case history, someone must uncover what went wrong, what decisions were made, which obstacles had to be managed, and how the individual’s judgment affected the outcome.
AI can help organize those answers, but it certainly cannot independently live through the experience, question the people involved, evaluate the evidence, or decide which detail changes the reader’s understanding.
That is where my work sits.
I am not competing to produce the greatest number of words in the shortest amount of time, because that contest has already been decided.
The value lies in knowing what the document needs to accomplish, where the reader becomes confused, what information is missing, which claims require evidence, and how the facts should be arranged so the meaning becomes clear.
Therefore, the writing comes afterward.
The middle is where generic communication lives
Gary’s warning about the disappearing middle may be especially important for communication businesses.
The middle is crowded with writing that is technically acceptable but professionally forgettable. Why? Because, it is the agent biography which is filled with phrases such as “dedicated to exceptional service” without explaining what that dedication looks like in practice.
It is the listing description that could be attached to hundreds of similar homes.
It is the closing announcement that congratulates the clients but tells the reader nothing about what the agent did.
It is the automated LinkedIn message that pretends to be personal because the recipient’s first name was inserted into the opening line.
On the one hand, this kind of communication may still be grammatically correct, and on the other, it may even look polished. But you k now what? It simply has no real experience underneath it.
As AI makes this material easier to produce, the supply will grow, and the more of it people encounter, the less attention they will give it. But the good thing is that that does not mean professional writing becomes unnecessary. Instead, it means generic writing becomes less valuable while observed, reported, and carefully considered communication becomes more valuable.
The difference will not always be found in the elegance of the sentences. More interestingly, it will be found in the quality of the thinking that came before them.
The comments were not really about nostalgia
The discussion beneath Gary’s newsletter added another layer to the argument. For example, one of the persons who left a comment on the article, described returning to an analog watch because it allowed him to be more present. Another said running clubs had begun replacing traditional networking events. Other commenters mentioned concerts, dinners, offices, resale clothing, tactile design, restaurants, and the feeling of interacting with people who know your name.
At first glance, these examples may appear to be expressions of nostalgia, but I do not think that is what they are.
People, for example, are not necessarily trying to return to an earlier decade. What they are trying to recover, I believe, are attention, presence, texture, recognition, and a sense of belonging.
Most of all, they want to feel that they are somewhere rather than merely connected to something.
And as a communicator, I see the same need existing in real estate communication too.
A buyer, for argument's sake, does not necessarily want to feel processed through a system, and like wise:
A seller does not want to receive an update that could have been sent to twenty other clients.

• A prospective client reading an agent’s profile wants to understand the person behind the credentials.

• A LinkedIn connection does not want to discover that the thoughtful-looking message was generated and distributed to hundreds of people.
People simply want evidence that somebody noticed them, and that, in my humble understanding, is why my relationship-development work cannot be based on volume. For example, I do not need more connections simply for the sake of increasing the number displayed on my profile. What I do need, however, is more conversations with people whose work I have taken the time to understand.
Therefore, the purpose of my research is not to create the appearance of familiarity; but rather to determine whether there is a legitimate reason for the relationship to begin.
And so, it is my belief that people should feel researched, not targeted. Most of all, they should feel understood, not marketed to.
And therefore, as automated outreach becomes more common, a thoughtful comment or relevant question will become more noticeable because it demonstrates something increasingly rare: attention.
My version of the barbell
The barbell model gives me a clearer way to think about the future of Whyte-Hall Communications Network.
On one end is technology. AI can, for example, help me review large amounts of material, organize research, compare documents, identify repeated language, preserve relationship history, develop working drafts, and distribute findings across several publications.
Simply, it can and does make the operating system move faster and more consistent.
On the other end is the human work. That includes interviews, direct observation, professional judgment, conversations with agents and brokers, document reviews, case histories, reporting, relationship development, and the accumulated experience that helps me recognize when something does not make sense.
Neither end should be neglected, because without technology, the business may become unnecessarily slow and time consuming. Besides, without the human work, it becomes another content-production system capable of generating language without understanding the people or events behind it.
If you ask me, I believe the strongest position is not to choose between artificial intelligence and human judgment. Rather, it is to use technology to strengthen work that begins in the real world.
The industry is the studio
Gary’s idea of the store as a studio gives me another useful model for the business I am building.
My studio is not a room filled with lights, microphones, and cameras, but instead, the real estate industry itself. There you find that that it is…

• the agent profile that sounds like every other profile on the brokerage website.

• the closing that required months of careful work but was reduced to three sentences and a photograph of a key.

• the press release that contains an announcement but no clear news angle.

• the client letter that answers the writer’s question while leaving the reader’s question unresolved.

• the conversation with an agent who knows the work was difficult but has never been asked to explain why.
Those moments are not simply defects to criticize. They are evidence of where communication has failed to carry the full value of the work.
A closing, for example, does not become a meaningful case history simply because the transaction is complete. Someone must uncover what went wrong, what decisions were made, which obstacles had to be managed, and how the professional’s judgment affected the outcome.
That is where I see my role as something of a Sherlock Holmes. I examine where communication has broken down, determine why those failures matter, and help real estate professionals present their work so clearly that readers are not left to fill in the gaps themselves.
